newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Blair rolls out red carpet for Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Blair rolls out red carpet for Clinton.

text.p: President Bill Clinton flew into London on Thursday for talks with new Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair aimed at relaunching Britain's special relationship with the United States.
A beaming Blair, accompanied by his wife Cherie, greeted Clinton and his wife Hillary on the steps of his 10 Downing Street residence in bright sunshine.
"It's a beautiful day," Clinton said as he posed for the massed ranks of photographers and cameramen.
"Bill and Tony" already enjoy a warm personal relationship and the visit has been extended at Clinton's request from a brief stopover to a full day to give him more time with Blair.
Apart from his formal business, Clinton has set aside time to have fun in London. A round of sightseeing is pencilled in as well as dinner with the Blairs at a restaurant.

Clinton, the first foreign leader to phone Blair after his landslide election victory on May 1, has made no secret of his admiration for the British premier, whose Labour party had called on the Democrats for electioneering expertise.
Clinton, who flew into Heathrow airport from the Netherlands, has described Blair as an exciting and able man. "I like him very much," he said.

Blair is honouring Clinton by inviting him to say a few words to his assembled cabinet ministers at the end of their weekly meeting -- -- an honour previously given only to President Richard Nixon in 1969.
British officials said the official talks would cover ideas for job creation, NATO, Hong Kong and Northern Ireland.

Blair intends to encourage Clinton to keep using his influence to prevail on the Irish Republican Army to declare an unequivocal ceasefire in its long violent campaign to oust Britain from Northern Ireland.
In return, Blair will tell Clinton that the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, would be given a seat at talks on the future of the province "without unnecessary delay", an official said.
Britain is also keen to discuss plans for Bosnia after the planned withdrawal next year of NATO's peace-keeping force, which includes large U.S. and British contingents.
Aides said Blair was keen to capitalise on the interest that Labour's victory, which ended 18 years of Conservative rule, had sparked in the United States and elsewhere.
"He is well aware that the honeymoon won't last forever but that while it does, he intends to use it for Britain's advantage and to stamp Britain on the world map" Blair's spokesman said.

Clinton's ties with defeated prime minister John Major were cordial but he never forgot the help Major's Conservative party gave to his Republican rival George Bush in the 1992 race for the White House.
It was a far cry from the strong personal bonds President Ronald Reagan established with "Iron Lady" Margaret Thatcher.

Although it is premature to say Blair and Clinton will strike up a similar understanding, they enjoy a good personal chemistry and share many political ideas, especially over education, welfare and job creation policies.

After 18 years of mistrust between the British Conservative government and the European Union, Blair has sought to make a fresh start with his continental partners, stressing negotiation not confrontation.
On his visit last week to Washington, new Foreign Secretary Robin Cook said this did not mean neglecting transatlantic ties.
"Britain as a leading player in Europe would be a more useful partner to the United States than one that was drifting into being a marginalised offshore island," Cook said then.
